papers.title: Waveform morphology links local circuit kinetics to cortical interactions
papers.abstract: How does local cortical physiology shape interactions between brain regions? We combined neural mass modelling with human and macaque intracranial recordings to examine how synaptic kinetics link oscillatory waveform morphology to cortical interactions. In a modified excitatory-inhibitory Wilson-Cowan model, synaptic rise and decay kinetics shaped waveform geometry and phase-dependent responsiveness. Local kinetics and coupling symmetry jointly influenced interaction measures and temporal irreversibility, while phase-locked perturbations altered imaginary coherency and bivariate irreversibility even when the coupling strengths remained fixed. In stereo-EEG from 23 patients, waveform asymmetry was most strongly associated with local irreversibility, whereas mean instantaneous alpha frequency showed stronger associations with interregional measures. Subdural macaque electrocorticography reproduced the frequency associations but not the local waveform association. Together, these findings show that waveform shape carries information about local neuronal dynamics, provide a mechanistic framework for interpreting cortical interactions, and motivate testing waveform morphology as a guide to stimulation timing.

papers.title: Age-dependent changes in the putamen transcriptome and proteome of a transgenic minipig model of Huntington's disease
papers.abstract: Huntington's disease is an inherited neurodegenerative disorder with no disease-modifying treatment available. Preclinical trials of gene therapies rely on large animal models and the transgenic Huntington's disease (TgHD) minipig is one of them. Minipigs live more than a decade, so the effect of a single dose of gene therapy can be followed for years. The TgHD transgene carries a mixed CAG/CAA repeat that is not expected to expand somatically. However, its putamen, part of the striatum that degenerates first in patients, had not been examined by genome-wide methods, nor beyond 4 years of age. We compared the putamen of transgenic and wild-type minipigs at 4 and 8 years by RNA sequencing and label-free mass spectrometry proteomics, and measured mutant huntingtin by immunoassay. Seven genes were differentially expressed at 4 years and 3,324 at 8 years, and the pathway changes of the transcriptome and the proteome were concordant at that age. The D2 medium spiny neuron marker gene set was reduced at 8 years in both the transcriptome and the proteome. Mitochondrial and oxidative phosphorylation pathways were positively enriched at 4 years and negatively enriched at 8 years. Immune and complement pathways were positively enriched at 8 years, and the number of altered splicing events increased almost fivefold between 4 and 8 years. We detected no age-dependent accumulation of soluble mutant huntingtin. Since the repeat does not expand, these changes developed without somatic expansion, a major driver of progression in human Huntington's disease. We propose that the reduced neuronal markers reflect a loss of neuronal identity rather than neuronal death. The TgHD minipig would then recapitulate the slow early phase of the disease, when treatment is arguably most likely to help.

papers.title: An isogenic human stem cell model reveals NGLY1-dependent control of microglial development
papers.abstract: NGLY1 is a cytosolic N-glycanase involved in glycoprotein quality control and proteasome-mediated protein degradation and is critical for normal brain development and function. Although neuronal alterations caused by NGLY1 deficiency have been extensively characterized in animal and human cell models, how NGLY1 deficiency affects human glial cells, particularly microglia, the brain-resident innate immune cells, remains largely unknown. Using patient-derived NGLY1-deficient human induced pluripotent stem cell (hiPSC) lines and their corresponding CRISPR-mediated gene-corrected isogenic lines, we found that NGLY1-deficient primitive macrophage progenitors (PMPs) exhibited increased GlcNAc-Asn (GNA) accumulation and elevated expression of RUNX1, a key transcription factor regulating myeloid lineage development, accompanied by abnormal proliferation. Following further differentiation, NGLY1-deficient human microglia exhibited reduced morphological complexity and impaired phagocytic capacity. In addition, NGLY1-deficient microglia showed increased expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines, including IL-1{beta}, IL-6, and TNF, under both basal and stimulated conditions, indicative of a heightened inflammatory state. Mechanistically, our data showed that RUNX1 upregulation induced by NGLY1 deficiency partially mediated impaired PMP proliferation and subsequent microglial abnormalities, implicating RUNX1 dysregulation in NGLY1-associated microglial dysfunction and identifying RUNX1 as a potential therapeutic target. Together, using patient-derived and gene-corrected isogenic hiPSCs, our study establishes a human stem cell platform for modeling NGLY1 deficiency and reveals that impaired deglycosylation alters human microglial developmental trajectories and ultimately compromises microglial homeostasis and function. These microglial abnormalities may contribute to the neurological deficits observed in patients carrying loss-of-function variants in NGLY1.

papers.title: A four-dimensional single-cell and spatial atlas of cAMP-driven repair after rat spinal cord injury
papers.abstract: Cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) induction through photoactivatable adenylate cyclase (bPAC) in corticospinal neurons enhances locomotion after spinal cord injury (SCI); however, the molecular and cellular mechanisms that underlie this improvement are unknown. Here we perform single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) and spatial transcriptomics (ST) of spinal cord sections at the injury site of dorsal hemisected rats, to identify the pathways through which bPAC stimulation exerts its regenerative cues after SCI, along with the changes in cellular populations that occur in different parts of the spinal cord.

papers.title: State-dependent gating of sensory and cortical inputs by median raphe neurons
papers.abstract: The mesopontine median raphe (MnR) plays an important role in regulating brain states, hippocampal network activity, and memory processes. Recent studies have revealed that the MnR comprises three major neuronal populations: serotonergic (5-HT), glutamatergic (Vglut3-expressing), and GABAergic neurons. How these distinct neuronal populations may gate sensory and cortical inputs across different brain states remains largely unknown. Here, we combined in vivo electrophysiological recording, sensory or optogenetic stimulation, and transgenic approaches to characterize the response properties of 5-HT, Vglut3, and GABAergic MnR neurons during wakefulness and sleep. We found that MnR neurons exhibited pronounced state-dependent responses to both sensory and cortical stimulation, with response amplitudes significantly greater during slow-wave sleep than during wakefulness. Auditory and somatosensory stimuli elicited fast responses in the MnR: 5-HT neurons were primarily suppressed, whereas Vglut3 and GABAergic neurons were primarily activated, suggesting the presence of direct inputs from sensory thalamic or brainstem structures. Retrograde tracing identified several brainstem structures and, notably, the medial prefrontal cortex as sources of direct projections to the MnR. Optogenetic stimulation of prefrontal inputs to the MnR evoked inhibition of 5-HT neurons but robust excitation of Vglut3 neurons during slow-wave sleep, suggesting top-down control of MnR activity by the prefrontal cortex. Together, these findings reveal that the MnR exhibits enhanced sensitivity to both ascending sensory and descending cortical inputs during sleep, suggesting that it may integrate environmental and cortical signals to regulate hippocampal network activity and gate sleep-dependent memory processing.

papers.title: Inter-protocol reproducibility of multi-shell diffusion MRI metrics across major neuroimaging study protocols
papers.abstract: Diffusion MRI is a core component of large-scale neuroimaging initiatives, yet the reproducibility of quantitative dMRI metrics across different acquisition protocols remains unclear. We acquired seven multi-shell diffusion protocols representative of major consortia and clinical settings on a single scanner in 41 healthy adults, isolating protocol effects from hardware and site variability. A linear mixed-effects model was used to estimate the inter-protocol coefficient of variation (CV) and the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) for diffusion tensor imaging (DTI), diffusion kurtosis imaging (DKI), and standard model imaging (SMI) metrics across atlas-based white matter regions. Rank agreement was assessed with Kendall's W, and repeated scans of one protocol provided a reference for test-retest variability. Overall, inter-protocol variability was low, with median CVs of 2.9-6.1% for DTI, 3.7-5.0% for DKI, and 3.0-4.7% for SMI metrics. Protocols ranked subjects consistently (W = 0.73-0.86) but agreed less in absolute value (ICC = 0.31-0.66), with fractional anisotropy (FA) being the most stable metric. Acquisition parameters, including TE, b-values, and signal-to-noise ratio jointly explained 53-93% of the inter-protocol variance. Differences in the b-values used for DTI and DKI estimation were particularly important for the diffusivities: matching b-values across protocols reduced the median inter-protocol CV for MD from 5.0% to 1.8%, with smaller reductions for mean kurtosis (MK), axial kurtosis (AK) and the axonal water fraction (f). These findings demonstrate good reproducibility of quantitative higher-order diffusion MRI metrics across commonly used multi-shell acquisition protocols, which can be further improved by aligning b-values, providing a foundation for data pooling, harmonization, and normative modeling in large-scale neuroimaging studies.

papers.title: Motor cortex facilitates visual action override through the superior colliculus
papers.abstract: Unexpected visual events can leave goal pursuit undisturbed or trigger visual action override - an interruption that redirects behaviour towards the stimulus. Using a visual distraction task in freely moving mice, population calcium recordings and causal perturbations identified the lateral motor-related superior colliculus (lSCm) as a key node controlling distractor engagement. Retinal inputs to the sensory-related SC signalled distractors even when mice ignored them. Pre-distractor behaviour and motor cortical activity predicted subsequent engagement, while increased corticocollicular and decreased nigrocollicular activity before distractor onset were consistent with a permissive state for override. Suppressing corticocollicular transmission weakened override without detectably altering task engagement. Single-unit recordings in head-fixed mice revealed response amplification in subsets of lSCm neurons during combined retinal and motor cortical stimulation, despite weak responses to either input alone. Motor cortical input thus facilitates sensory recruitment of collicular action circuits, shaping the balance between action stability and action override during ongoing goal pursuit.

papers.title: Tracking single neurons across days reveals acute and persistent effects of psilocybin in the mouse brain
papers.abstract: The psychedelic psilocybin offers a novel approach to treat depression and other psychiatric disorders. A single dose of psilocybin induces rapid neuroplastic effects that persist for many weeks to months. However, psilocybin's effect on neural firing beyond its systemic presence, and the neural mechanisms linking these acute and sustained effects remain unknown. Using chronically implanted Neuropixels probes, we tracked 1,692 neurons spanning prefrontal and hippocampal regions following saline and psilocybin injections and 24 h later. Psilocybin bidirectionally modulated firing acutely in a cell-type and region-specific manner. Persistent firing (24 h post-injection) is net suppressed relative to saline, including in acutely activated neurons. The late acute response, but not early peak response, predicted a neuron's firing 24 h later. To our knowledge, this is the first evidence that directly reveals psilocybin's sustained impacts on neuronal firing, providing key insight into the circuitry accompanying its lasting cognitive and behavioral alterations.

papers.title: Visual Illusion: A Matter Of Disorder Between Retinal And Perceived images
papers.abstract: Visual illusions reveal that perception is constructive rather than a faithful copy of the retinal image. This paper proposes that the brain supplements ambiguous or incomplete sensory input with virtual edges, filled-in surfaces, brightness and size cues, and illusory contours. Using gray-level Shannon entropy, we compared original and perceived images across five illusion classes: edge detection, surface filling-in, brightness perception, size perception, and the Hermann grid. In all cases, perceived-image entropy exceeded real-image entropy. These findings support a unified account of visual illusions as constructive inference: the brain introduces additional information to achieve global coherence, reflecting a trade-off between low-entropy processing and perceptual interpretation.

papers.title: NeuroMASS v4: Geometry-Aware Neural Population Dynamics via Learnable Hyperbolic Latent Representations and Biologically-Calibrated Diagonal State Space Models
papers.abstract: The geometry of neural population activity is a fundamental challenge in computational neuroscience. We present NeuroMASS v4, a novel architecture that introduces learnable hyperbolic latent geometry to spike-train co-smoothing on the Neural Latents Benchmark (NLB'21). Our central scientific claim is that the curvature c of a Poincar&eacute-ball--learned end-to-end from extracellular spike recordings--constitutes a biologically interpretable geometric signature: significantly positive for ring-manifold motor circuits (MC_Maze, MC_RTT) and near-zero for topologically unstructured frontal circuits (DMFC_RSG). The architecture unifies five principled components: (i) discrete spike-count embed- dings with learned neuron-identity vectors, (ii) permutation-equivariant attention-weighted neuron pooling, (iii) a diagonal S4D state space model initialised with a log-uniform frequency prior spanning 2-200 Hz, (iv) a Poincar&eacute-ball projection with learnable scalar curvature, and (v) a Frobenius-bounded session adapter. Training uses masked self-prediction of spike counts with an auxiliary behaviour decoding objective; all experiments use exclusively real DANDI/NLB recordings under a strict fail-stop data policy. We report results across four NLB datasets spanning motor, somatosensory, and cognitive cortices in rhesus macaque, and demonstrate that learned curvature statistically predicts circuit topology.

papers.title: Circuit decoupling with surrogate compensation for baseline tuning in biophysically detailed neural models
papers.abstract: The baseline regime of a neural circuit shapes its dynamical behavior. Establishing an appropriate baseline is therefore an important part of tuning a computational circuit model. This baseline can be specified in terms of target population firing rates and achieved by adjusting the background inputs to each population. Due to recurrent coupling, these inputs need to be tuned jointly, requiring a high-dimensional search that is especially costly for biophysically detailed circuit models. This remains a major bottleneck since current optimization methods are limited in their ability to tackle this problem. Decoupling the circuit by removing all the connections between its cells allows background inputs to be tuned independently, but the solution may not hold when the connectivity is restored. We developed a compensated decoupling method in which missing recurrent inputs are replaced by surrogate inputs from spike generators firing at the corresponding target rates. The resulting input approximates the recurrent drive expected at the target regime, so the background inputs tuned in this setup may remain valid after restoring connectivity. We applied the method to a 43-population biophysically detailed model of the macaque auditory thalamocortical circuit, which had previously proved challenging to fit closely to experimental data. First, we tuned the background input independently for each population in the fully decoupled setup. Next, we tested the solution in the isolated cortical and thalamic subcircuits, preserving recurrent connections within each subcircuit. The cortical subcircuit had two coexisting regimes and settled into the off-target one by default. A gradual transition from surrogate to recurrent self-excitation allowed it to reach the near-target regime. The thalamic subcircuit exhibited a single regime deviating from the target due to imperfect surrogate compensation. Jointly tuning a separate tonic input correction for each thalamic population substantially reduced the errors. Finally, we tested the solution in the full thalamocortical circuit, combining the tuned background inputs, thalamic corrections, and gradual restoration of self-excitation. The full circuit consistently reached a near-target regime across multiple random model realizations. The approach yielded an improved macaque auditory thalamocortical baseline model, providing a community resource for investigating the auditory thalamocortical system's dynamics. Together, the results demonstrate that our method can facilitate baseline tuning in a biophysically detailed model by enabling decoupled optimization and guiding subsequent refinement.

papers.title: Longitudinal examination of cerebellar morphometry across typical aging adults reveals nonlinear heterogenous trends
papers.abstract: Cerebellar structural integrity has been associated with cognitive capability in both neurodegenerative and healthy aging populations. The understanding of regional, longitudinal cerebellar structural changes is not well studied, and with an increasing aging population, there is an increasing need to fill this gap. Moreover, traditional modeling approaches apply linear techniques, which may fail to detect possible nuanced aging patterns. The present study investigates the nonlinear effect of age on subregional cerebellar structures in healthy adults (n = 1,371), aged 36 to 90+, from the Human Connectome Project in Aging and the follow-up continuation, Aging Adult Brain Connectome studies. Subject T1w images underwent cerebellar segmentation and volumetric estimation via the Automatic Cerebellum Parcellation using U-NET with Locally Constrained Optimization (ACAPULCO) algorithm. Cross-sectional, longitudinal, and sex specific volumetric differences were examined using generalized additive mixed models. Heterogenous atrophy patterns were observed across the cerebellum; however, the majority of effects were evident in the posterior cerebellum. Longitudinal models showed nonlinear negative trends for all regions surviving correction, while baseline age effects had a combination of linear and nonlinear negative trajectories after correction. Specific sex differences emerged, where men predominantly had higher regional volumes, as well as there being sex-related influences of longitudinal morphologic patterns. Furthermore, midlife appeared as a period of structural vulnerability, demonstrating escalated volume loss. Consistent with the literature, the identified volumetric reduction patterns suggest that age effects on the cerebellum are multifaceted, with region specific alterations, highlighting the complexity of this structure.

papers.title: Preparatory Bias Currents Alone Write Letters and Words in a Fixed Recurrent Circuit
papers.abstract: We show that preparatory input currents, or bias currents, alone can make a recurrent circuit with fixed weights write all 52 cursive letters, and words built from them. Each letter is produced by its own bias pattern, ramped in as a preparatory drive and withdrawn at a go cue; the recurrent weights and the readout never change, and the readout's weights are random, with a single global gain picked on four letters (a-d). We take the stability-optimized circuits (SOCs) of Hennequin et al. and extend them with mutual inhibition: all inhibitory neurons inhibit one another through a single shared weight (MISOC, mutual inhibition SOC). With 200 units, the pen of the SOC stays on average 1.7% of a letter width from the target over all 52 letters, and that of the MISOC 0.9% (25 random circuits; R2 = 0.996 and 0.999). The other 48 letters are learned through their bias patterns alone, without changing a single synapse, so new letters cannot disturb old ones. Letters learned one at a time chain into words in one continuous run. Mutual inhibition improves the circuit: with a shared weight of 0.5 the MISOC writes with 16-48% less error than the SOC at every network size tested (50 to 200 units), and with fifty network-derived input channels instead of one bias per neuron it keeps its advantage. Bias currents and mutual inhibition let small, fixed circuits hold a large and growing motor repertoire and switch within it without any synaptic change.

papers.title: Structure learning and context inference emerge from next-state prediction in a cerebellar-medial temporal lobe circuit
papers.abstract: Humans learn many context-dependent behaviors; yet the contexts driving these behavior are rarely explicit and must instead be inferred. Further, we are rarely exposed to the same context multiple times, so we must learn how to generalize to new contexts from our experiences in prior ones. Motor learning relies on both. People can hold multiple conflicting visuomotor mappings and recall the appropriate mapping when needed. Much as cricket is easier to learn for someone who already plays baseball, experience with previous mappings accelerates learning of others. Indeed, human motor learning is well described by context inference, in which the learner infers the context and uses it to update and recall the appropriate memory. How the brain implements this inference, and which circuits perform it, however, is unknown. Here we introduce a circuit in which a cerebellar forward model predicts the next state conditioned on a latent from the medial temporal lobe. At the same time, the medial temporal lobe updates that latent from the cerebellum's prediction error. While we only trained the circuit to predict next state, it learns to infer context and represents contexts in a structured latent space. Coupled with this latent, a motor cortex module reproduces context-dependent retrieval, savings after washout, spontaneous recovery, and evoked recovery, and compensates for perturbations it has never experienced. The same circuit reproduces cerebellar-dependence of object-location memory and independence in object-recognition memory, loss of place-cell stability in the dark when cerebellar plasticity is blocked, and the abstract geometry of hippocampal activity in a reversal task. Cerebellar-medial temporal lobe interaction is therefore a candidate locus for context inference and structure learning in the brain.

papers.title: A digital twin of freely moving mouse V1 learns a general visual code bridging classical physiology and active vision
papers.abstract: Decades of controlled experiments in passive, head-fixed animals have characterized the response properties of mouse primary visual cortex (V1) and their strong modulation by behavioral state. However, in natural vision the animal is active, continuously shaping its own visual input as it moves and coupling vision to behavior. To bridge this gap between classical controlled experiments and natural vision, we trained a multimodal digital twin to predict V1 spiking in freely moving mice from retinocentric video together with locomotion, pupil, and eye and head movements, then froze it and probed it in silico under controlled conditions. The representation it learned generalized across stimulus classes, animals, and recording regimes. Although never trained on parametric stimuli or given cell-type labels, the model recovered V1's canonical tuning for orientation, spatial frequency and contrast, including the systematic differences between putative excitatory and inhibitory cells. A single model transferred to new mice from a few minutes of recording. Without retraining, it matched the representational geometry of an independent head-fixed dataset of natural movies as closely as two recorded mice match each other. Behavior modulated most V1 neurons, and clamping each variable in turn showed that locomotion and pupil dilation share a gain increase, while only locomotion shifts sensitivity toward high spatial frequencies. By learning this representation from the freely behaving animal and probing it under controlled conditions, freely moving digital twins bridge classical visual physiology and active vision.

papers.title: α-Synuclein structural heterogeneity associates with distinct cytopathologies in multiple system atrophy
papers.abstract: Multiple system atrophy (MSA) is characterized by oligodendroglial -synuclein inclusions, although neuronal inclusions also occur. We investigated whether regional differences in -synuclein filament structure are associated with distinct cytopathologies in a neuropathologically confirmed MSA brain by comparing the medial temporal lobe, which showed prominent neuronal inclusions and limited oligodendroglial pathology, with cerebellar white matter, which contained exclusively oligodendroglial inclusions. Cryo-electron microscopy resolved filaments from these regions at 3.0 [A] and 2.0 [A], respectively. Medial temporal filaments contained a previously undescribed protofilament fold, PF-IIIA, paired with canonical PF-IIB2, whereas cerebellar filaments adopted the canonical MSA Type II structure. PF-IIIA exhibits extensive remodeling of its core while retaining the asymmetric doublet architecture. These findings reveal regional -synuclein structural heterogeneity within a single MSA brain and suggest a potential association between distinct filament conformations and neuronal versus oligodendroglial cytopathology, highlighting the importance of regional and cellular context in filament organization and disease heterogeneity.

papers.title: Learning predictive latent structure from unclustered neural spike trains
papers.abstract: Neural activity patterns enable perception, thought, and action. A powerful approach to understanding these abilities involves identifying low-dimensional, interpretable latent variables that capture the relationship between activity patterns, the information they represent, and the computations they support. Yet current methods often yield variables that are difficult to interpret and require data preprocessing that limits their accuracy and temporal resolution. Here we introduce Contrastive Prediction of Point Process Observations (C3PO), an unsupervised method that learns a predictive, interpretable latent variable representation directly from continuous time neural spiking without requiring spike-sorting or binning. C3PO recovers structure associated with known latent variables across a variety of data sets without access to those variables during training. It identifies dynamics on timescales from tens of milliseconds to hours and reveals previously unreported representations and their dynamics. These results establish C3PO as a powerful tool for uncovering interpretable structure in high-dimensional point-process data sets.

papers.title: Bullying Victimisation, Medial Occipital White Matter Development, and Psychotic-Like Experiences: A Longitudinal Diffusion MRI Study
papers.abstract: Childhood bullying victimisation is robustly associated with psychotic-like experiences, but the neurodevelopmental mechanisms underlying this association remain unclear. This longitudinal study examined whether childhood bullying victimisation was associated with altered maturation of medial occipital white matter and whether bullying victimisation moderated the association between fractional anisotropy (FA) and psychotic-like experiences. A total of 96 young people (38 bullied, 58 controls) from the Adolescent Brain Development study underwent diffusion MRI at approximately 14, 16, and 20 years of age. PLE and bullying victimisation group classification were determined by expert consensus interview. FA from bilateral calcarine-cuneus, cuneus-lingual, and calcarine-lingual connections was examined using mixed-effects models. Compared with controls, the bullied group showed significantly different age-related FA trajectories in the right calcarine-cuneus connection ({beta} = -0.40, p < .001) and the left cuneus-lingual connection ({beta} = -0.35, p = .003). Bullying victimisation significantly moderated the association between white matter FA and PLE ({beta} = -6.14, p = .004), indicating that the association between FA and psychotic-like experiences differed according to bullying victimisation status. This moderation effect also varied with age, as indicated by a significant bullying victimisation-by-FA-by-time interaction ({beta} = -6.80, p = .008). Specifically, the moderating effect of bullying victimisation on the association between right calcarine-cuneus FA and PLE changed across development. These findings suggest that bullying victimisation is associated with divergent maturation of medial occipital circuitry and identify right calcarine-cuneus development as a potential marker of vulnerability to PLE following childhood bullying.

papers.title: Dynamic information sharing across frontal-basal ganglia neurons during cost-benefit decision-making and reward pursuit
papers.abstract: Cost-benefit decision-making requires animals to integrate prospective rewards with the costs of obtaining them and translate these evaluations into motivated action. How population activity is coordinated across the frontal-basal ganglia network during these processes remains incompletely understood. Here, we recorded simultaneously from the anterior cingulate cortex, medial/ventral orbitofrontal cortex, dorsomedial striatum, ventral pallidum and subthalamic area in rats performing a cost-benefit decision task. Using canonical correlation analysis, we identified shared population activity across these anatomically distributed circuits and characterised its dimensionality, task-related information and relationship to behavioural sensitivity. The strength and dimensionality of inter-area coupling varied across task epochs and circuit classes, with frontal-basal ganglia interactions exhibiting particularly high dimensionality during reward pursuit. Shared activity represented reward and time on task (trial count) during decision-making, while movement-related information became increasingly prominent during reward pursuit. These representations also depended on subsequent choice: reward was more strongly represented on accepted trials, whereas time on task was more prominent on rejected trials. The strength of inter-area coupling was further associated with behavioural sensitivity across sessions. Stronger coupling between the subthalamic area and the dorsomedial striatum was associated with reduced reward sensitivity. By contrast, communication between the medial/ventral orbitofrontal cortex and dorsomedial striatal was associated with reduced effort aversion. Together, these findings reveal a dynamic, circuit-specific organisation of shared neural activity during cost-benefit behaviour and link inter-area coupling to variation in motivated choice. They suggest that distinct communication pathways may contribute to specific facets of motivated choice, with applications to targeted neuromodulation therapies for disorders of motivation.

papers.title: Parvalbumin interneuron circuit sharpens orientation tuning via the extraclassical surround in cat V1
papers.abstract: Parvalbumin-expressing (PV) inhibitory neurons are central to cortical gain control, yet optogenetic studies disagree on whether they sharpen orientation tuning or merely rescale responses. Because this work has been performed almost exclusively in rodents, which lack orientation columns and an orientation-matched extraclassical surround, the contribution of surround circuitry has remained untested. Here we combine cell-type-specific rabies-virus tracing with optogenetics to activate or suppress PV circuits in cat primary visual cortex, and measure single-neuron orientation tuning for stimuli confined to the classical receptive field or extending into the extraclassical surround. Activating PV circuits sharpened tuning progressively with illumination power for classical-receptive-field stimuli, but left tuning unchanged once the surround was engaged; conversely, suppressing them broadened tuning only for surround-engaging stimuli and left classical-receptive-field tuning unchanged. This double dissociation places PV circuitry in the causal path that sets tuning width and identifies surround suppression as the inhibition it supplies: where the surround is not recruited there is little PV-mediated inhibition to remove, and where it is, removing that inhibition widens tuning. PV-dependent sharpening is therefore bounded by the receptive-field architecture through which the population is recruited, not by a fixed property of the PV population itself.

papers.title: Schizophrenia-Linked 3q29 Deletion Produces Hyperdopaminergic Signaling in the Dorsal Striatum
papers.abstract: Dopamine dysregulation has long been recognized as a central feature of schizophrenia (SZ), yet the mechanisms linking genetic risk to dopaminergic dysfunction remain poorly understood. While pharmacological models have historically been used to induce hyperdopaminergic states and recapitulate select clinical features of SZ, these approaches do not model the underlying disease biology. In contrast, genetically informed models enable investigation of dopaminergic abnormalities as emergent consequences of bona fide disease-associated mechanisms. Here, we examined a mouse model of the 3q29 deletion. In humans, this 1.6 Mb deletion is typically de novo and confers a greater than 40-fold increased risk for SZ, representing the single largest known molecular risk factor for the disorder. Using this model, we identified a robust hyperdopaminergic phenotype characterized by elevated evoked dopamine release selectively within the dorsal striatum. Mechanistically, this phenotype appears to arise from a PKC-mediated reduction in dopamine transporter (DAT) availability, impairing dopamine clearance and prolonging dopaminergic signaling. Together, these results establish a direct link between a high-risk SZ mutation and striatal dopamine dysfunction, while also highlighting PKC-DAT signaling as a potential therapeutic target for treatment-resistant neuropsychiatric symptoms associated with 3q29 deletion.

papers.title: Harmonizing amyloid PET tracers at the local level: evaluation of regional Centiloid equations
papers.abstract: INTRODUCTION: The Centiloid (CL) framework standardizes global amyloid-PET across radiotracers. While global scaling remains essential for participant selection, amyloid-targeting therapies require quantifying localized plaque removal. However, applying global equations regionally introduces systematic bias, particularly in subcortical structures where off-target binding alters non-specific background. METHODS: We extended the Centiloid framework regionally and voxel-wise using GAAIN datasets: Level-1 ([11C]PiB) and Level-2 paired [11C]PiB and fluorinated head-to-head cohorts ([18F]florbetaben, [18F]florbetapir, [18F]flutemetamol, and [18F]NAV4694). Level-1 defines the regional Centiloid scale using region-specific intercepts while fixing the global slope. Level-2 calibrates fluorinated tracer uptake to reference [11C]PiB SUVR using linear equations. We compared three slope-intercept models (Global, Regional-Intercept, and Regional) using information criteria and Mean Absolute Error (MAE). RESULTS: Regional-Intercept model was identified as optimal across all four radiotracers. In neocortical regions, Global and Regional-Intercept models showed high agreement across canonical lobes. In deep gray matter, global equations introduced large systematic offsets, with mean absolute conversion errors in the pallidum reaching 27.7 to 45.6 CL. The Regional-Intercept model eliminated this bias, reducing subcortical MAE on average below 15 CL while preserving a unified biological scale. DISCUSSION: Applying global Centiloid equations directly to regions introduces substantial bias in subcortical regions. With the Regional-Intercept model, the same Centiloid value corresponds to the same amyloid concentration across brain regions and radiotracers. This provides a reliable basis for cross- sectional regional evaluation, multi-tracer cohort pooling, tracking regional clearance, and mapping regional progression in clinical research.

papers.title: Geometric analysis of postnatal maturational transformations in brain's functional connectome
papers.abstract: Birth marks a profound shift in sensory experience, posing a question: does postnatal brain function represent simply a protracted continuation of prenatal developmental programmes or reflect system-level reconfiguration in response to the demands of the postnatal environment? To answer this, we first characterised functional hierarchies of the newborn human brain, separating sensorimotor from visual, unimodal from associative, and parietal from auditory systems. We then implemented a geometric framework to map global transformations that shape functional connectome hierarchies. We show that greater postmenstrual age at birth was associated with emergence of the frontoparietal and salience networks at the tip of the unimodal-associative hierarchical axis; in contrast, greater postnatal age was associated with increasing polarisation of primary perceptual and sensorimotor systems across functional hierarchies. Sex differences in the neonatal connectome recapitulated patterns associated with postmenstrual age at birth and postnatal age, suggesting more advanced maturation of functional architecture in females than in males. Together, the contrasting effects of prenatal and postnatal age support a model of postnatal reconfiguration of brain function, thereby indicating that birth could mark a transition between distinct modes of the functional organisation.

papers.title: The social conditioned place preference assay is sensitive to drug dose, training regimen, and social context
papers.abstract: Beginning in the 1960s, researchers have understood that one of the unique properties of psychedelic drugs is that their effects are modified by the context in which they are taken (also known as their set and setting dependence). To date, 7 different studies have shown that critical period reopening is a shared property across psychedelic drugs, including ketamine, MDMA, psilocybin, LSD, and ibogaine. Moreover, the context dependence of psychedelics effects has been recapitulated for both MDMA and ketamine. Recently, Lu et al., Nature Neuroscience 2026 (PMID: 42972049) have claimed that psilocybin does not reopen the social reward learning critical period, which the authors interpret as a failure to replicate previously published results. Here, we re-analyzed results across three published datasets (Nardou et al., Nature 2019; Nardou et al., Nature 2023; Lu et al., Nature Neuroscience 2026) in order to compare the impact of dose, training regimen, and social context on the social conditioned place preference (social CPP) assay. Our analysis reveals that methodological modifications likely account for Lu and colleagues inability to reopen the social reward learning critical period with psilocybin. Nevertheless, because their results recapitulate previous findings that psychedelics effects are context dependent, they support rather than challenge the growing literature demonstrating that psychedelics reopen critical periods.

papers.title: Engineered post-transcriptional regulation of Scn10a by Pumilio ameliorates neuropathic pain in mice
papers.abstract: Post-transcriptional control of mRNA permeates biology, yet its contribution to sensory neuron physiology and pain remains unclear. The mammalian Pumilio proteins PUM1 and PUM2 (collectively referred to as PUM) are RNA-binding proteins that bind Pumilio response elements (PREs), typically situated in 3' untranslated regions. PUM recruits the CCR4-NOT complex to promote mRNA deadenylation and decay. Several mRNAs that encode voltage-gated sodium channels that regulate action potential generation in pain sensing neurons harbor PREs. Here, we explored whether PUM plays a role in pain signaling. PUM1 and PUM2 were enriched in TRPV1-positive dorsal root ganglion neurons, where PUM2 physically interacted with Scn9a, Scn10a, and Scn11a transcripts, which encode Nav1.7, Nav1.8, and Nav1.9, respectively. Depletion of PUM in sensory neurons produced mechanical hypersensitivity and enhanced inflammatory pain. These effects were reversed by blocking Nav1.8 but not Nav1.7, raising the possibility that repression of Scn10a by PUM can be harnessed using synthetic biology to diminish neuropathic pain. To this end, we generated a chimera comprising the RNA-binding domain of PUM2 and a repressive domain, which we dubbed "super-PUM". Expression of AAV-encoded super-PUM in sensory neurons reduced Nav1.8 abundance, diminished tetrodotoxin-resistant and suzetrigine-sensitive sodium currents, and prevented mechanical and thermal hypersensitivity following spared nerve injury. These results demonstrate that optimization of an endogenous post-transcriptional regulon provides a means to ameliorate neuropathic pain.

papers.title: The ANKLE2-VRK1 pathway promotes neuronal resilience by preserving proteostasis during aging
papers.abstract: ANKLE2 is a key regulator of neural stem cell division through inhibition of the kinase VRK1, and mutations in either ANKLE2 or VRK1 cause rare neurodevelopmental disorders that impact brain growth and development. Recent evidence showing that reduced ANKLE2 activity promotes Tau aggregation in vitro suggests that ANKLE2 may also contribute to age-related neurodegenerative processes; however, its role post-development remains unknown. Using Drosophila, we show a novel role for the Ankle2-ballchen (VRK1) pathway in maintaining neuronal resilience and proteostasis. Pan-neuronal and motor neuron reduction of Ankle2 in adult animals shortens lifespan, impairs motor function and accelerates neuronal loss. Lifelong reduction produces more severe phenotypes including an upright wing posture reminiscent of Drosophila Parkinsons disease models. Mechanistically, loss of Ankle2 causes the accumulation of ubiquitinated proteins throughout the central nervous system, indicating impaired protein clearance. Ankle2 mutants have reduced proteasome activity with activation of compensatory degradative pathways, supporting this hypothesis. Loss of Ankle2 behavioral and protein accumulation phenotypes are rescued by expression of human ANKLE2, indicating neuronal ANKLE2 function is conserved between flies and humans. Importantly, VRK1/Ballchen reduction also rescues ubiquitin accumulation and behavior phenotypes caused by loss of Ankle2, demonstrating that the developmental Ankle2-VRK1 pathway is preserved and remains functionally important in aged neurons. More broadly, our findings reveal that a conserved developmental ANKLE2- VRK1 pathway is repurposed in aged neurons to maintain proteostasis and neuronal resilience, providing a mechanistic framework linking neurodevelopmental disease genes to age-associated neurodegeneration.

papers.title: Constrained Geometric Approach for Robust Local Optic Axis Estimation with Single Input Polarization Sensitive Optical Coherence Tomography
papers.abstract: Polarization-sensitive optical coherence tomography (PSOCT) enables label-free, depth-resolved microstructure mapping in biological tissues, making it a powerful tool for studying myelinated fiber structures in the brain. Conventional single-input PSOCT measures cumulative retardance and apparent optic axis, which become inaccurate when fibers cross over depth. In single-input PSOCT systems, local optic axis estimation is challenging due to high noise levels, limiting the reliability of depth-resolved orientation estimation. In this work, we present a robust framework for local optic axis estimation in single-input PSOCT that incorporates physical constraints and polarization super-pixels. Polarization super-pixels serve as a preprocessing step to cluster spatially connected pixels with similar polarization states, increasing the effective signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) and reducing instability in recursive matrix inversion. In addition, a physical constraint based on the mirror state of the input polarization is enforced during geometric fitting, significantly improving robustness and accuracy under noisy and low-SNR conditions. Experimental validation on ex vivo human brain tissue and phantoms demonstrates substantially improved stability and robustness of local optic axis estimation. This work enables reliable depth-resolved fiber orientation mapping in sophisticated fiber crossing scenarios and extends the potential of single-input PSOCT for analyzing structural connectivity at high depth resolution.

papers.title: The role of shape and local features in human object recognition and learning
papers.abstract: An object's shape is an important visual cue, critical for both perception and cognition. However, the current best models of human vision, Deep Neural Networks (DNNs), do not prioritize shape, but instead, they rely on texture-like local visual features. This raises the question: Could shape be less important for human perception than previously believed? In seven experiments with both adults (N = 300) and 5-year-old children (N = 100), we tested the role of shape and local features in visual object recognition and learning. We found that humans could identify common objects as accurately using local visual features as they could using shape. This finding suggests that, like DNNs, local features may be sufficient for everyday visual recognition and that shape may not be necessary. However, we found that shape played a crucial role in novel object learning, allowing participants to even accomplish one-shot object categorization. Together, these findings force us to reconsider the role of shape in visual recognition and suggest that DNNs, despite not using shape, may nevertheless capture an important aspect of human visual processing.

papers.title: Preserved cognitive control with altered ventromedial prefrontal activity in lichen simplex chronicus: an fMRI study during the Multi-Source Interference Task.
papers.abstract: Lichen simplex chronicus (LSC) is a chronic pruritic skin condition, and one of its central features is the itch-scratch cycle. It has been hypothesized that resisting the urge to scratch, and thereby stopping this cycle, may depend on mechanisms of cognitive control. Here, we used the Multi-Source Interference Task (MSIT) during fMRI to examine whether patients with LSC (n = 9) differ from healthy controls (n = 11) in interference control or in the brain activity that supports it. Our results show that both groups had the expected interference effect, with no statistically significant group differences in behavioral performance or in cingulo-frontal-parietal BOLD activity. Whole-brain analysis revealed a greater interference-related decrease in ventromedial prefrontal cortex activity in patients than in controls. These exploratory findings show distinct patterns of brain activity in LSC while preserving interference control, warranting further investigation in larger samples.

papers.title: Restrictive eating is linked to weaker recollection of food in young adults
papers.abstract: Affective significance often enhances episodic memory, with stronger effects on recollection than on familiarity, but prior research has focused primarily on within-person manipulations of emotional valence. Here, we tested a novel question: whether stable individual differences in the personal significance of food were associated with long-term memory across individuals, given that food ranges from highly appetitive to strongly avoided. Across two experiments, we examined familiarity-based memory (using an image recognition task) and recollection-based memory (using a spatial source recognition task) for food and nonfood stimuli as a function of eating-related individual differences in young adults. In Experiment 1, familiarity-based recognition memory was largely unrelated to eating behavior. In Experiment 2, however, greater restrictive eating and fear of negative consequences from eating were associated with poorer recollection-based memory for food when compared to nonfood stimuli. Together, these findings suggest that individual differences in the affective significance of food do not correlate with episodic memory uniformly but instead are selectively associated with reduced recollection, but not familiarity, of food relative to neutral stimuli.
